text: A wealthy household decides that what one of its sons needs is a woman it can hire. Khilona spends 160 minutes inside one family's house, where a poet has been kept locked on the terrace since the night the woman he loved was married to somebody else, and where a courtesan named Chand is brought in and told to sit with him. The treatment works, after a fashion. What follows is the arithmetic nobody in the house is willing to do aloud: she was engaged to repair a son, she has no standing to ask for anything, and the household finds her presence hardest to bear exactly when it is working. Melodrama at this length can let an arrangement rot slowly instead of breaking it. The Filmfare for best film of 1970 went to a picture whose sharpest attention is on the people doing the paying.

Popielawy is a village, and a Polish film of 1998 is named for what it claims happened there. Jan Jakub Kolski works in a register that lets a farmyard hold the impossible without anybody raising their voice about it: romance, country drama and open fantasy declared together inside a hundred minutes. The combination is harder to bring off than it sounds. Wonder set among rural people either condescends to them or credits them with invention and appetite, and the difference becomes legible almost at once. Kolski takes the second road, and the Polish Film Award for best film followed. Whatever marvel he proposes is kept at village scale, measured in wood, weather, animals and one person's stubbornness rather than in spectacle, which is a rarer thing on film than the marvel itself.

A baron finds a drunk asleep in his field and cannot let the chance pass. Jeppe is carried up to the castle, dressed in the baron's finest bedclothes and laid in the baron's bed, and when he wakes he takes it for the afterlife, at which point the lackeys patiently correct him downward, until he accepts that he is the baron himself. He believes it in stages. That is the comic part and also the cruel one, because everything he then does with his new authority, the old scores settled and the old appetites indulged, is being performed for men who arranged it and will be telling the story next week. The Bodil for best actor in a leading role went to the performance at the centre of that, a part obliged to be pitiable and insufferable inside the same sentence.

The war is over, the garrison is not, and the officers are left with a rank, a ration and nothing to do with either. Pyotr Todorovskiy sets Encore, Once More Encore! in a distant garrison town at the turn of the Fifties and lets the conditions do the work: drinking that begins earlier each week, authority exercised over trivia, soldiers serving out duties that have mislaid their reason. It is filed as comedy as much as drama, which is not a filing error; the humour is the kind that circulates in a closed place where everyone knows everyone's business and none of it may be said aloud. Feeling breaks out anyway, between people with no room to have it, and the town has practised methods for putting it down. It took the Nika for best picture.

Racehorses first, and the people who cannot stay away from them second. Kira Muratova gives Lilia and Violetta, one fair, one dark, introduced almost as a matched pair and then declining to behave like one, a track to circle, and the young riders there circle back toward them. What passes between them is not quite a plot; it is a run of encounters that keep sliding out of ordinary realism and then back into it, tender in one scene and abrupt in the next. The photography is the other subject: horses, light, movement, given an attentiveness the human talk is not granted. 112 minutes, in Russian, 1994. It took the jury and critics prizes at Kinotavr. Neither woman is asked to explain what the track gives her, and no explanation is supplied on her behalf.

Three ages of one boy, eighty-six minutes, and no plot to speak of. Nils Malmros builds Drenge out of separate episodes, a small boy with a cousin lodged in the house, a schoolboy in love past the point of dignity, a young man working on a nurse, and the interest sits in the gaps, since nothing carries across but the person. Denmark put it forward as its international submission to the Academy Awards. What it watches is the machinery of wanting at an age when the wanting is the whole event and its object hardly has to exist as a person; what it withholds is the lesson usually attached. Boys here are frequently unpleasant, and the film neither punishes nor excuses them. It stays in the room a little longer than is comfortable.

An animated feature about a murderer who becomes a knight, made in Hungary in 1984 and plainly not intended for children. Daliás idők takes a man whose enormous strength is the only quality anyone has ever valued in him, sets him running from a killing, and then finds a use for him: armour, a lord, a war. Drawing a battle instead of filming one changes what it costs. Every horse, every crowd, every wound is a deliberate mark somebody made, so the atrocity arrives already interpreted; nothing is caught by accident, and across eighty-three minutes that accumulates. The Cristal at Annecy went to it, from the one festival that judges this kind of work on its own terms. Disillusion is not the destination here. It is a stage on the itinerary, with a good deal of road after it.

The competition comes once in ten years, which gives a dancer perhaps three chances in a working life. Mangal Maharaj intends his son to take this one, and everything after that proceeds from a technical requirement: the Shiv-Parvati Tandav cannot be danced alone. A partner has to be found, drilled and kept in condition to appear, so a father's ambition turns into an arrangement with a young woman's life inside it, and turns into something harder when Neeladevi and Girdhar stop being colleagues. 143 minutes, 1956, with the training given as much screen time and as much strain as the performance it is for. The Filmfare for best film went to it. What the picture grasps is that in this form discipline and desire draw on the same faculty and will not separate on request.

A car that does not run, in the yard of a dairy farm in the Danish marshes, and an apprentice who works on it in the hours when he is not milking. Carl-Henning's world is as small as board and lodging make a world, and it comes apart over one evening: beer, money lifted from the till, a foreman's fists, a staircase. He runs. The cruel joke of Lene Grønlykke's film is that the damage behind him is slight and the pardon real, but no word of either travels far enough to reach him, so a misunderstanding hardens into a life, a travelling carnival first and then wherever the carnival goes. Eighty-five minutes, 1969, and Denmark's international submission to the Academy Awards. It is unusual mainly in how little it wants to blame anyone for any of it.

A man comes in out of the rain, is given a bed for the night, and is still there the next day, and the day after that. Johan Jacobsen's film keeps to one house, one woman living alone in it, and a guest who never quite supplies a reason for staying. Ninety minutes is time enough for hospitality to settle into routine, and for routine to become something that would have to be named before it could be ended. The charge comes from what neither of them says: she does not ask who he is, and each day she does not ask commits her further to not asking. Falling in love, when it arrives, is less a turn in the story than a word for what has been true for several days. Denmark, 1959, two people, and the weather doing the rest.

A boy arrives in Copenhagen from the country looking for work, and finds that his face is worth more to certain people than his labour. Bundfald is eighty-six minutes about a small racket run on thin margins: a group of young men use him as bait, and the money comes from older men who cannot go to anyone afterwards. Palle Kjærulff-Schmidt is less interested in the crime than in the apprenticeship, in how quickly someone with no wages and no address learns the part assigned to him, and how the people teaching it regard it as a trade like any other. The film is from 1957, and it treats the city as an economy with a bottom, where shame is the raw material and everyone working in it knows the current price.

Fifteen years after the occupation ended, a Danish film went back to the resistance and took suspicion rather than sabotage as its subject. An English agent arrives by plane, is hurt on arrival, and has to be hidden and nursed by a cell already too small to spare anyone. Then the operations begin failing the same way each time: the Germans are there first, or nearly. Ninety-one minutes is a tight frame for that arithmetic, and it pushes the film indoors, into who was told, who left early, who has relatives in a position to be leaned on. The Bodil for best Danish film went to it. The weight is in the cost of a correct assumption: once a cell decides one of its own is informing, it must go on working as though nobody is, each man beside a person he is quietly measuring.

The Filmfare for best film of 1972 went to a domestic drama with a company deep enough to fill a stage. Manoj Kumar and Raakhee lead; Premnath, Pran, Prem Chopra and Tun Tun take up the rest of Be-Imaan's 133 minutes, which is a great many speaking parts for a story about what relatives owe one another. That material only works at length: money lent and never mentioned again, a place kept at a table, decisions taken on somebody's behalf and announced afterwards. Shankar Jaikishan wrote the music, and in Hindi cinema of these years the songs are not ornament but the place where the case gets made. Sohanlal Kanwar directed. The title comes down written in both Devanagari and Nastaliq, an accurate picture of the language these films actually spoke.

The tour ends in Rio, which is her business and not his, until he decides otherwise. A dancer and a Danish student fall into conversation on a train, and the film lives in the gap between two readings of that hour: for her a pleasant stretch of a journey, for him grounds to cross an ocean. Henning Carlsen shot it in Danish for a Swedish production in 1967, ninety-five minutes out of a Jens August Schade novel, and the crossed borders of the production suit a story in which distance is the smallest of the obstacles. It went forward as an international submission to the Academy Awards. The comedy, if that is what it is, sits in the disproportion: nothing said on that train obliged him to follow, and the pursuit has to invent its own justification as it travels.
